analysis.one_liner: Raises federal oil and gas royalties and rents, ends noncompetitive leasing, and protects surface landowners from drilling damage.
analysis.headline: A House committee passed the bill 20-15 in September 2020, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how the federal government leases public land for oil and gas drilling. It would end the practice of handing out leases to a single noncompetitive bidder, raise the minimum royalty companies pay on oil and gas extracted from public land from 12.5% to at least 18.5%, roughly double annual rental rates, and shorten lease terms from 10 years to 5. It would also give private landowners sitting above federal minerals new rights to negotiate with, and get compensated by, drilling companies, and require the Interior Department to publish who holds and trades federal oil and gas leases. The committee reported it in December 2020, but no floor vote ever came.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would collect more money for oil and gas taken from land they own, and private landowners whose ranches and farms sit on top of federally owned minerals, who would gain negotiated agreements, damage compensation, bonds, and notice before drilling begins.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum federal royalty on oil and gas from public lands to at least 18.5%, up from the century-old 12.5% rate, so taxpayers get a larger share of the value of resources they own.
Eliminates noncompetitive leasing, under which a single company could claim a lease without any auction, and requires sealed competitive bidding instead.

Raises annual rental rates to at least $3 per acre for the first two years and $5 per acre after, and lets the Interior Secretary raise rates further to improve financial returns to the United States.

Requires drilling companies to reach a written surface use agreement with private landowners above federal minerals before drilling, covering limited land use, reclamation, and compensation for lost income, damaged property, and unreclaimed sites, with operator-paid arbitration when no agreement is reached.

Requires notice to surface owners and the public at least 45 days before lease sales and 30 days before drilling permits or lease modifications, and lets surface owners participate in bonding decisions and request inspections.
Requires a public website listing every current and former lessee and operator on each federal lease, every transfer, and every suspension of operations or production.

Lets the Interior Secretary adopt master leasing plans to sort out in advance where drilling fits and conflicts with conservation, recreation, and cultural resources, and requires such a plan when a state, county, or petitioning resident asks for one.
Bars new oil shale leasing until technical and economic feasibility of development has been demonstrated.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land, who would pay higher royalties and rents, win leases only through sealed competitive auctions, hold shorter leases, negotiate with surface owners, and disclose their identities and lease transfers publicly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land

drawbacks.text: Higher royalties and rents and shorter lease terms could make some federal parcels uneconomic to drill, reducing drilling activity and the federal leasing revenue that comes with it, the standard industry objection to leasing reform.

The surface use agreement requirement, with bonding and arbitration, would add time and cost before operators could drill on split-estate land, and companies could be authorized to drill only after a 90-day good-faith process if no agreement is reached.
The bill imposes a fee just to submit an expression of interest in leasing, which could make it slightly more costly for small or first-time prospective bidders to participate.
Lease sales would be limited to no more than three per state per year and each field office's lands offered once a year, slowing the pace of leasing compared with the quarterly schedule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is money: companies pay more, taxpayers and landowners get more. The royalty increase alone would return a meaningfully larger share of publicly owned oil and gas to the Treasury, and the landowner provisions address a real gap, since owners of the surface above federal minerals currently have limited leverage when a company holds the right to drill beneath them. The main costs fall on the drilling industry and, at the margin, on the pace of federal drilling. The bill is deliberately structured to raise the price of leasing, so its benefits and costs are two sides of the same mechanism rather than a hidden tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: The Natural Resources Committee passed it 20-15 and reported it to the House floor in December 2020, but leadership never scheduled a vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, killing the bill.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Mike Levin on June 12, 2019 and referred to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees.
It gained 22 Democratic cosponsors in the House during the Congress.
The Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 20-15 on September 30, 2020, after a subcommittee hearing in June 2019.

The committee reported the bill on December 24, 2020 (H. Rept. 116-689), the Agriculture Committee was discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, meaning it was eligible for a floor vote.
The House never took up the bill, and all legislation pending at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the status quo: the 12.5% royalty, noncompetitive leases, 10-year terms, and limited landowner leverage over drilling beneath their property.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 22 Democratic cosponsors; it passed his committee 20-15.

for.name: Rep. Raul Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as chair he brought the bill through subcommittee, a markup that passed 20-15, and a December 2020 committee report to the House floor.

against.name: 15 House Natural Resources Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting no at the September 30, 2020 markup
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported, 15 no votes to 20 yes.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a floor vote; the bill sat on the Union Calendar for the final days of the Congress and expired.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was 20-15 in a committee chaired by a Democrat, and all 22 cosponsors were Democrats; the record does not give the party breakdown of the vote, but no House Republicans cosponsored.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal lands
industries.note: The bill raises their costs on public-land drilling: royalties up to at least 18.5%, doubled rentals, sealed-bid auctions only, 5-year leases, surface-owner agreements, and public disclosure of who holds and trades leases. The industry's interest in keeping the current cheap, quiet leasing terms runs against the taxpayers and landowners who would gain.

The bill bars new oil shale leases until feasibility of development is demonstrated, closing off speculative federal leasing. The public would forgo nothing proven and avoid leasing land for development that may never be economic.

industries.industry: Surface landowners above federal minerals (ranchers and farmers)
industries.note: Split-estate landowners would gain required surface use agreements, compensation for crop, livestock, and income losses, bonding they can petition against, and notice of leasing and permitting decisions. They are the everyday people the bill is named for.
